name: Immutability
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Why You Can't Just Erase a Mistake
lesson.summary: Immutability means that once data has been added to a blockchain and accepted by the network, it cannot be altered or deleted without being detected, because doing so would break the chain of cryptographic hashes.
lesson.body:
"Immutable" is one of the most overused words in blockchain marketing, and it is worth being precise about what it actually means, because the precise meaning is more interesting and more limited than the marketing version. Immutability does not mean a blockchain is physically impossible to alter. Anyone with access to the underlying files could, in principle, edit a byte on their own copy. What immutability means is that altering past data is immediately and mathematically detectable, and that undoing the detection would require redoing an enormous amount of prior work across a majority of a distributed, replicated network.

This rests on the hash chain structure introduced earlier. Each block in a blockchain contains a cryptographic hash, a short fixed length fingerprint, of the block before it. Because a cryptographic hash changes completely and unpredictably if even one bit of the input changes, altering a transaction buried deep in the chain's history would change that block's hash, which would no longer match the reference stored in the next block, which would break that block's hash too, and so on all the way to the most recent block. The chain does not merely record history, it cryptographically welds each entry to the ones before it.

Immutability also depends on the distributed ledger property covered earlier: many independent copies. A hash chain alone, sitting on one computer, could simply be regenerated from a chosen point forward by whoever controls that computer, since nothing stops them from recalculating every hash after their edit. What actually protects the historical record is that thousands of other nodes hold their own copies of the original chain, and a lone edited copy will not match the majority. On networks that use proof of work, rewriting history also means redoing the computational effort for every block from the edit point onward, faster than the rest of the network is adding new blocks, which becomes exponentially harder the deeper the edit sits in the past.

A concrete illustration: suppose a transaction recorded ten thousand blocks ago sent 5 coins from Alice to Bob, and someone wants to quietly change it to 5 coins from Alice to themselves. They would need to alter that block, which changes its hash, which no longer matches what block 10,001 recorded, requiring them to also alter block 10,001, and 10,002, and every block since, all before honest nodes extend the real chain any further. On a network of any real size, this is not merely difficult, it is computationally infeasible within a human timescale.

The honest caveat: immutability is a property of accepted, deeply buried history, not of anything written to the chain a moment ago. Very recent blocks can occasionally be reorganized during ordinary network operation before they are considered final, which is why services often wait for several confirmations before treating a transaction as settled. And immutability guarantees that data was not secretly altered, it says nothing about whether the data was true, fair, or legal when it was written. An immutable record of a fraudulent transaction is still immutable, and still fraudulent.
